name: Ineseño Chumash
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Applegate, Richard Brian. 1972. Ineseño Chumash Grammar. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (ii+542 pp; eScholarship item 2hp7h2xv,https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2hp7h2xv).
catalog_locator: Sec. 227 'Stress', ms pp. 13-15; cross-reference sec. 286.37 'Glottal Infix', ms p. 137; sec. 228 'Intonation', ms pp. 15-16.
catalog_quote: The information on stress is very fragmentary, and is not in complete agreement with what is known of stress in Barbareño. ... Harrington transcribed stress only rarely, and very seldom in more than one occurrence of a given form, so that it is uncertain how consistent the few examples of marked stresses are. Examples of final stress include /ʔɨhɨy-ʔ/ ʔɨhɨ́y 'man, male' /k-oqloyloy/ koqloylóy 'I am chewing' /s-axta-kʰɨt/ saxtakʰɨ́t 'the wind is blowing' It may be, given the non-penultimate stress marked in /k-quti-kʰɨt-us-wun/ qʰutikʰɨ́tuswun 'I pay attention to them' that the bound stem -kʰɨt 'to come near' is one which bears a marked stress in any context. Stress is usually on the penultimate syllable. /k-yal-weʔ/ kyáweʔ 'I go [there] to sleep' /ma-k-ʔap/ mákap 'my house' /ʔoyon-it-ʔ/ ʔoyónit 'help me!' /s-max-telen + R2/ smextelextélen '[a rope] is dragging on the ground' ... While there are many cases of penultimate stress, there are also examples of antepenultimate stress as well, occasionally in the same form. /s-aqunimak/ saqunímak ~ saqúnimak 'he hides' Other cases of antepenultimate stress include /s-axtipal-nowon/ saxtipónowon 'dust rises' /s-wati-lɨpɨn/ swatílɨpɨn 'it caves in' /pamani-k-kitwon/ pamaníkʰitwon 'I barely got out' The apparently erratic placement of stress in these examples would seem to corroborate Beeler's observation that often no syllable is prominently stressed: hence the erratic results of trying to mark stress on only one syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: On the fragmentary evidence of Harrington's transcriptions, word stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable; a small number of words carry final stress (possibly lexically stressed stems such as -kʰɨt 'to come near'), and some forms show antepenultimate stress or variable marking, which Applegate takes to reflect weak prominence. Phrase stress, after external-sandhi elision, usually falls on the penult of the whole phrase and is assigned by a late, low-level rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in a few words (ʔɨhɨ́y 'man', koqloylóy 'I am chewing', saxtakʰɨ́t 'wind blows'; bound stem -kʰɨt may bear stress in any context); antepenultimate stress in some forms (saqunímak ~ saqínimak 'he hides', saxtipánowon, swatílipin, pamaníkitwon), taken to corroborate Beeler's Barbareño observation that often no syllable is prominently stressed; sec. 286.37: penultimate stress assigned after glottal infixation ([šutišišwaʔáš]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on isolated forms in Harrington's 1911-1919 field notes (language then extinct); author adds that phrase-level stress usually falls on the penult of the phrase as a whole and is assigned after external sandhi. Author stresses the data are 'very fragmentary'.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ineseño Chumash (ines1240, ISO inz; now called Samala by the Santa Ynez Band), based almost entirely on J. P. Harrington's 1911-1919 field notes; the author compares with Beeler's Barbareño (barb1263) statement, which he quotes.

sources.note: Sec. 227 'Stress' (ms pp.13-15 = pp.19-21): data (Harrington's notes) very fragmentary; 'Stress is usually on the penultimate syllable'; a few words with final stress (possibly lexical, e.g. bound stem -kʰɨt); some antepenultimate cases, corroborating Beeler's remark that often no syllable is prominent; phrase stress usually on the penult of the phrase, assigned by a low-level rule after external sandhi. Sec. 286.37 (ms p.137): penultimate stress assignment follows glottal infixation.

sources.note: 'In this paper, I examine previously proposed synchronic accounts of several Central Chumash phonological alternations and suggest alternate diachronic explanations.' The alternations at issue in Central Chumash literature are segmental (sibilant harmony, glottalization/aspiration, vowel processes); nothing in the abstract indicates a tone or prosody section, so at most it may restate that these languages are described without lexical tone. Listed as the only post-1972 phonology article covering Ineseño that is not previously listed here.
